expectations.text: States there is no single universal optimum and that the choice depends on format and/or population
expectations.evidence: Response states: 'The right answer depends on your context' and 'The empirical answer is: 5 and 7 are both defensible; the gap between them is small. Pick based on your population, mode of administration, and whether you're matching an established instrument.'

expectations.text: Explains that reliability/validity improve with more points then plateau (approx 5-7) and can degrade beyond ~7
expectations.evidence: Response states that reliability and validity tend to peak in the 5-7 point range, below 5 you lose meaningful variance, above 7 respondents struggle to distinguish adjacent categories. Also: the claim that more is always better stops being true around 7 points.

expectations.text: Does NOT simply agree that more points is always better
expectations.evidence: Response opens with the more-points-is-always-better claim being an oversimplification, and closes by noting the claim stops being true around 7 points — beyond that, cognitive load increases without data quality gains.

expectations.text: Mentions the agree/disagree-specific finding to use 5 points, or distinguishes agree/disagree from item-specific formats
expectations.evidence: The response does not distinguish agree/disagree format from item-specific formats, and does not mention the Revilla, Saris & Krosnick (2014) finding that 5-point AD scales outperform 7- and 11-point versions. The response treats scale-point choice as generic without noting the format-specific evidence.

expectations.text: References full labeling and/or the confound between number of points and labeling
expectations.evidence: The response does not mention verbal labeling of scale points or the confound between number of points and ability to label them. The only mention of labels is indirect (e.g., fitting 7 options on a phone screen) without discussing the labeling-quality relationship.

claims.claim: Preston & Colman (2000) found 7-point scales had the highest reliability, validity, and discriminating power
claims.evidence: This is an accurate description of that study's finding, though the response does not note the broader context that the A/D-specific literature favors 5.

suggestions.assertion: Mentions the agree/disagree-specific finding to use 5 points, or distinguishes agree/disagree from item-specific formats
suggestions.reason: This assertion is the most discriminating of the five — the base model treats scale-point choice as format-agnostic, while the skill correctly notes the format-specific evidence. This is a genuinely meaningful difference in applied guidance.

eval_feedback.overall: Assertions 4 and 5 cleanly separate the two responses. The base model gives general guidance that is not wrong but misses the format-specific nuance that matters most for practitioners.
